items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Nijō Castle in Kyoto, Japan, has wooden corridors with “nightingale floors,” named for the birdlike chirps they emit underfoot.
• Each floorboard is fastened to the supporting beams with nails held in metal clamps.
• A footstep pushes the board down slightly, displacing the nails within their clamps.
• As each nail shifts, it rubs against its clamp, producing a high, chirping squeak.
• Visitors are frequently told the floors were designed to detect intruders, but the sound may have been unintentional.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how nightingale floors produce their sound. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: When someone walks on a nightingale floor, its boards bend and rub against one another, and this rubbing produces the birdlike chirp.
Each footstep on a nightingale floor makes the metal clamps vibrate against the beams below, and those vibrations produce a high, chirping squeak.
A footstep presses a board down slightly, shifting the nails that hold it so that they scrape against their metal clamps and chirp.
Visitors to Nijō Castle are often told that its nightingale floors, named for their birdlike chirps, were meant to warn of intruders.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain how nightingale floors produce their sound. The notes trace a chain: “A footstep pushes the board down slightly, displacing the nails within their clamps,” and “As each nail shifts, it rubs against its clamp, producing a high, chirping squeak.” Choice C follows that chain in its own words: the pressed board shifts the nails, which scrape against their clamps and chirp.

A.why_wrong: It explains the chirp as the boards rubbing against one another, but the notes say the sound comes from the nails: each one “rubs against its clamp.”

B.why_wrong: It names the clamps but has them vibrating against the beams; according to the notes, the squeak comes when each nail “rubs against its clamp.”

D.why_wrong: It reports what visitors are told about the floors’ purpose, which the notes say may have been unintentional, and does not explain how the floors produce their sound.

Subject: technology and history (nightingale floors, Nijō Castle, Kyoto). Mechanism and the hedge on intent as on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightingale_floor (flooring nails rub against a clamp; a sign at the castle says the sound is not intentional). No invented names or figures. Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped (boards rub each other), B FALSE goal-shaped (clamps against beams), D true but off-goal (the intruder story). Goal-only solve (without the notes): A, B and C all explain how.

key restates the chain in its own words (presses, shifting, scrape)
two goal-shaped FALSE options that keep the parts but swap which ones rub (board on board, clamp on beam)
one accurate OG option (the intruder story the notes hedge)

Without the notes, A, B and C all fit the goal.

items.subtype: Make and support a generalization (one level above the cases)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Paleontologists compare extinct island mammals with related mainland species to determine how body size changes on islands.
• The Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus, which disappeared about 10,000 years ago, weighed about 200 kilograms.
• The common hippopotamus, a close relative from mainland Africa, can weigh over 1,500 kilograms.
• Nuralagus rex, an extinct rabbit from the Mediterranean island of Menorca, weighed about 12 kilograms.
• The European rabbit, a relative from the nearby mainland, typically weighs less than 2 kilograms.
items.stem: The student wants to make and support a generalization about how island mammals’ body sizes can compare with those of related mainland species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
options: Island mammals can become either much smaller or much larger than related mainland species, as the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus and Menorca’s Nuralagus rex show.
Like the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus, which weighed a fraction of what its mainland relative does, mammals that colonize islands such as Menorca tend to shrink over time.
At about 200 kilograms, the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus weighed far more than Nuralagus rex, an extinct rabbit from Menorca that weighed about 12 kilograms.
According to paleontologists who study island mammals, both the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus and Menorca’s Nuralagus rex disappeared about 10,000 years ago.
items.explanation: The goal is a generalization, with support, about how island mammals’ sizes compare with related mainland species. The dwarf hippopotamus weighed “about 200 kilograms” against the common hippopotamus’s “over 1,500 kilograms,” while Nuralagus rex weighed “about 12 kilograms” against the European rabbit’s “less than 2 kilograms.” Choice A generalizes that island mammals can become either much smaller or much larger and cites both animals as support.

B.why_wrong: It makes and supports a generalization, but the generalization is wrong: Nuralagus rex, from Menorca, weighed far more than the European rabbit, so island mammals do not simply tend to shrink.

C.why_wrong: It compares the two island animals with each other rather than with related mainland species, and it makes no generalization.

D.why_wrong: The notes give the date of disappearance only for the Cyprus dwarf hippopotamus, and the sentence says nothing about body size.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (body-size change in island mammals). Real subject known without a search (WAVE.md: no fact-checking); the term “island rule” and the famous Flores cases are left out to avoid a topic-fame tell. Weights rounded (Cyprus dwarf hippo about 200 kg; Nuralagus rex about 12 kg). Option fact check: B FALSE goal-shaped, D FALSE conflation, C true but the wrong comparison.
band7_moves: generalization one level above the two cases (size can shift in either direction), derived from two pairs of weights the notes never compare
goal-shaped FALSE: a one-direction generalization supported by one case while the notes’ second case contradicts it
FALSE conflation that gives one animal’s date to both
a true wrong-comparison option (the two island animals compared with each other)

fixes: notes: 'usually weighs' to 'typically weighs' (keeps the hard tier at CB's long-word share after the 01 rewrite)

band7.why: The generalization climbs a level (size can shift either way) from two weight pairs the notes never compare; B is a goal-shaped make-and-support that the rabbit case contradicts, D a date conflation, C a true comparison of the wrong pair. Matches 3dcc7140 and 7f5715e4.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Guano, the accumulated excrement of seabirds, is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, nutrients essential to agriculture.
• On Peru’s arid Chincha Islands, guano had accumulated over centuries into deposits more than 30 meters deep.
• Beginning in the 1840s, Peru shipped millions of tons of it to Europe and the United States.
• For approximately three decades, these exports were the Peruvian government’s largest source of revenue.
• By the 1870s, the richest deposits were exhausted, and the guano boom ended.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of Peru’s guano boom. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Over centuries, guano rich in nitrogen and phosphorus accumulated on Peru’s arid Chincha Islands in deposits more than 30 meters deep.
From the 1840s to the 1870s, guano exports provided much of Peru’s revenue, until cheaper fertilizers from other countries brought the boom to an end.
Beginning in the 1840s, Peru shipped millions of tons of guano to Europe and the United States, where it was used to fertilize crops.
From the 1840s until the richest deposits ran out in the 1870s, guano exports brought the Peruvian government more revenue than any other source.
items.explanation: An overview should span the boom from start to finish. Choice D gives its start (“Beginning in the 1840s”), its importance (the exports were “the Peruvian government’s largest source of revenue,” which D restates as more revenue than any other source) and its end, when “the richest deposits were exhausted” in the 1870s.

A.why_wrong: It explains how the guano deposits formed, which comes before the boom, and says nothing about the exports or how the boom ended.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: wrong cause of the end)
B.why_wrong: It spans the whole boom, but the notes say it ended because “the richest deposits were exhausted,” not because of cheaper fertilizers from other countries.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the exports began but says nothing about their importance to Peru or how the boom ended.

items.notes: Subject: history (Peru’s nineteenth-century guano boom). Real subject known without a search (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill); figures kept round (deposits more than 30 m deep, millions of tons, about three decades).
band7_moves: overview spanning the arc (start, importance, end and its cause) in one sentence
goal-shaped FALSE: a full-arc overview that gives the wrong cause for the end
two accurate PART options, each covering one stage of the arc

fixes: key D paraphrased ('brought the Peruvian government more revenue than any other source') so it no longer copies the notes' 'largest source of revenue'; explanation updated

band7.why: Keeps 964c6055's PART, PART shape and adds a goal-shaped FALSE full-arc overview (wrong cause of the end); the key now restates the revenue bullet instead of copying it. Borderline: A and C are quick rejections, so the item rests on B.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In southern Niger, the rainy season lasts approximately 90 days; millet still ripening afterward yields little grain.
• Researchers there grew two new varieties of pearl millet alongside a traditional variety in a drought year.
• The traditional variety matured in about 110 days; Varieties 1 and 2 matured in about 80 and 85 days.
• Variety 1 produced 30% more grain than the traditional variety; Variety 2 produced 25% more.
• Variety 1 also had shorter stalks, which farmers often use to feed livestock.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of a similarity between Varieties 1 and 2. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Since Varieties 1 and 2 each produced 30% more grain than the traditional variety did, farmers could expect either one to outperform it in a drought year.
Varieties 1 and 2 both mature in less time than the rainy season usually lasts, so unlike the traditional variety, they can ripen before the rains end.
In the researchers’ trial, Varieties 1 and 2 matured within about five days of each other.
Varieties 1 and 2 both have shorter stalks than the traditional variety does, which may make them less useful to farmers who feed stalks to livestock.
items.explanation: The goal is the significance of a similarity. Varieties 1 and 2 “matured in about 80 and 85 days,” both less than the rainy season’s “approximately 90 days,” while the traditional variety needed “about 110 days.” Because millet “still ripening afterward yields little grain,” Choice B gives the shared trait and why it matters: both new varieties can ripen before the rains end.

A.why_wrong: Only Variety 1 produced 30% more grain than the traditional variety; Variety 2 “produced 25% more,” so the stated similarity is wrong.

C.why_wrong: It notes that the two varieties matured at about the same time but never says why that matters.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: one variety’s trait given to both)
D.why_wrong: The notes say only that “Variety 1 also had shorter stalks”; nothing is said about Variety 2’s stalks.

items.notes: Subject: natural science and agriculture (early-maturing pearl millet in the Sahel). Unnamed, plainly generic study with invented figures (WAVE.md wave-3 lesson); no real study or variety named. Architecture differs from 19b08ead: two new varieties against one local check, and the significance comes from the length of the rainy season rather than from a ranking of three.
band7_moves: significance-of-a-similarity goal; the shared trait (maturing within the season) is derived by comparing numbers across two bullets
two goal-shaped FALSE options that state a similarity and a significance but give one variety’s figure or trait to both
a true similarity with no significance (C), as in 19b08ead

review.note: invented figures sit on an unnamed, plainly generic trial ('Researchers there'); no real study, institute or variety is named or identifiable

band7.why: Same architecture as 19b08ead: the significance of a similarity is derived by setting 80 and 85 days against the 90-day season and the 110-day local variety; A and D are goal-shaped FALSE similarities (a number and a trait given to both); C is a true similarity with no significance.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Latvian-born immigrant Annie Cohen Kopchovsky lived in Boston with her husband and three young children.
• In June 1894, she departed Boston on a bicycle, intending to circumnavigate the globe.
• A spring water company paid her to display its advertisement, and she adopted its name, Londonderry.
• Traveling by bicycle, steamship, and train, she crossed portions of Europe and Asia before returning to America.
• She completed the journey in September 1895, approximately fifteen months after she set out.
items.stem: The student wants to begin a narrative about Kopchovsky’s journey around the world. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In June 1894, Annie Cohen Kopchovsky, a Boston mother of three, set off on a bicycle with an ambitious plan: to travel around the world.
Sponsored by a Boston newspaper, Latvian-born immigrant Annie Londonderry pedaled out of the city in June 1894, bound for a trip around the world.
By September 1895, Kopchovsky, who had taken the name Londonderry from a spring water company, had completed her trip around the world.
Traveling by bicycle, steamship, and train, Annie Londonderry crossed portions of Europe and Asia before returning to America.
items.explanation: A narrative should start at the beginning of the story. Choice A opens at the chronological start, “In June 1894,” introduces Kopchovsky as a Boston mother of three, and sets up the trip around the world she began when she “departed Boston on a bicycle,” leaving the rest of the story to follow.

B.why_wrong: It opens at the right moment, but the notes say “A spring water company paid her to display its advertisement,” not a Boston newspaper.

C.why_wrong: It starts with the end of the journey in September 1895, which suits a conclusion rather than the opening of a narrative.

D.why_wrong: It describes her route partway through the trip without first introducing her or the start of the journey.

items.notes: Subject: history (Annie Cohen Kopchovsky, known as Annie Londonderry). Real subject known without a search (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill); only core, widely reported facts used (left Boston in June 1894 on a bicycle, a spring water company’s sponsorship and name, finished in September 1895).
band7_moves: narrative-opening goal over notes that run identity, start, sponsor, route, end
goal-shaped FALSE: an opener at the right moment that misstates the sponsor, recast so it no longer mirrors the key
OG jump to the outcome and a PART from the middle of the trip

fixes: option B recast ('Sponsored by a Boston newspaper, ... pedaled out of the city in June 1894') so it no longer mirrors the key's 'In June 1894, Annie ..., a ...' frame; same single false fact (the sponsor)
notes: 'after departing' to 'after she set out' (hard tier chars per word back under CB + 0.20)
review.note: real person; only her widely reported journey facts, no invented finding

band7.why: af88c47a's OG and PART shape plus one goal-shaped FALSE opener (wrong sponsor), now recast so it does not mirror the key; the key opens at the chronological start. Borderline: C and D are quick rejections.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tivaevae are colorful quilts sewn collaboratively by women in the Cook Islands, often as ceremonial gifts.
• A tivaevae taorei is pieced together from thousands of small fabric squares.
• Its patterns, frequently floral, are assembled square by square.
• A tivaevae manu features one large design cut from folded fabric and stitched onto a contrasting background.
• Its designs are also frequently inspired by flowers.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in how the two kinds of tivaevae are made. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both tivaevae taorei and tivaevae manu frequently have designs that are inspired by flowers.
Although both are quilts from the Cook Islands, a tivaevae taorei and a tivaevae manu are made in very different ways.
Tivaevae, colorful quilts sewn collaboratively by women in the Cook Islands, are often given as ceremonial gifts.
Whereas a tivaevae taorei is pieced together from thousands of small squares, a tivaevae manu features one large design stitched onto a background.
items.explanation: The goal is a difference in how the quilts are made. A taorei is “pieced together from thousands of small fabric squares,” while a manu “features one large design cut from folded fabric and stitched onto a contrasting background.” Choice D sets the two methods side by side with “Whereas.”

A.why_wrong: It states something the two kinds of quilt share, designs inspired by flowers, rather than a difference in how they are made.

B.why_wrong: It says the two kinds are made in different ways but never says how either one is made.

C.why_wrong: It describes tivaevae in general and how they are used, without distinguishing the two kinds.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Cook Islands quilting). Real subject known without a search; no named people (WAVE.md). One shared trait (floral designs) feeds the REL option; one differing attribute (construction) is the goal.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The begena and the krar are Ethiopian lyres.
• The begena is a large lyre with ten strings and a deep, buzzing tone.
• It is traditionally played to accompany prayer and meditation, especially in the weeks before Easter.
• The krar is a smaller lyre with five or six strings and a bright tone.
• It is commonly played at weddings and other celebrations to accompany singing and dancing.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast the occasions on which the two lyres are typically played. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The krar, a smaller lyre with five or six strings, is commonly played at weddings and other celebrations.
While the begena traditionally accompanies prayer and meditation, the krar is commonly played at weddings and other celebrations.
The begena is a large lyre with ten strings and a deep, buzzing tone, whereas the krar is smaller, with five or six strings and a bright tone.
Both the begena and the krar are lyres that are played in Ethiopia.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast when the two lyres are played. The begena “is traditionally played to accompany prayer and meditation,” while the krar “is commonly played at weddings and other celebrations.” Choice B sets these occasions side by side with “While.”

A.why_wrong: It gives the occasions for the krar only; the begena is not mentioned, so there is no contrast.

C.why_wrong: It contrasts the lyres’ size, strings, and tone, not the occasions on which they are played.

D.why_wrong: It states what the two lyres have in common rather than contrasting when they are played.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Ethiopian music). Real instruments known without a search; no named people (WAVE.md). Two differing attributes in the notes (size and strings, occasion); the goal names one, and the other feeds the wrong-dimension option.

items.subtype: Describe a work to an unfamiliar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Gonkar Gyatso is a contemporary artist who was born in Lhasa, Tibet, in 1961.
• He trained as a painter in Beijing and later relocated to London.
• Many of his artworks depict the traditional seated figure of the Buddha.
• Rather than applying paint, he fills the outline of the figure with hundreds of colorful stickers.
• The stickers feature cartoon characters, corporate logos, and other imagery from popular culture.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Gyatso’s images of the Buddha to an audience unfamiliar with the artist. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Gyatso fills the outlines of his seated Buddhas with hundreds of colorful stickers featuring cartoon characters, corporate logos, and other imagery from popular culture.
Born in Lhasa, Tibet, in 1961, Gonkar Gyatso trained as a painter in Beijing before relocating to London.
Tibetan-born artist Gonkar Gyatso creates images of the seated Buddha by filling the figure’s outline with hundreds of stickers drawn from popular culture.
Contemporary artist Gonkar Gyatso, who was born in Tibet, uses unusual materials in his images of the Buddha.
items.explanation: An audience unfamiliar with Gyatso needs to learn who he is as well as what the images look like. Choice C identifies him as a Tibetan-born artist (he “was born in Lhasa, Tibet”) and describes the images: he “fills the outline of the figure with hundreds of colorful stickers” featuring “imagery from popular culture.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the images well but uses the name Gyatso without saying who he is, which an unfamiliar audience would need.

B.why_wrong: It introduces the artist’s background but never describes his images of the Buddha.

D.why_wrong: It identifies the artist but says only that he uses “unusual materials,” without describing the stickers or what they show.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Gonkar Gyatso, Tibetan-born contemporary artist known for sticker collages of the Buddha). Real artist known without a search (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill); only widely reported facts used (born in Lhasa in 1961, studied in Beijing, later lived in London, Buddha figures filled with pop-culture stickers). No work titles or dates of works named.

review.note: real artist; only widely reported biography and the sticker Buddhas, no invented finding

items.subtype: Explain a process to an unfamiliar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Anthotypes are photographic images made with light-sensitive juices from plants.
• British scientist John Herschel developed the process in 1842.
• To make one, a photographer coats paper with juice crushed from flower petals, berries, or leaves.
• An object is positioned on the coated paper, which is then exposed to sunlight for days or weeks.
• Exposed areas of the coating fade, while covered areas retain their color, leaving an image.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how an anthotype’s image forms to an audience unfamiliar with anthotypes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: An anthotype, a photograph made with plant juices, forms as sunlight fades the exposed parts of the juice-coated paper while covered parts keep their color.
When an anthotype is left in sunlight, its exposed areas fade while the areas covered by an object keep their color.
British scientist John Herschel developed the anthotype, a kind of photographic image, in 1842.
To make an anthotype, a photographer coats paper with juice crushed from flower petals, berries, or leaves and then places an object on the coated paper.
items.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to learn what an anthotype is before the process makes sense. Choice A defines it as a photograph made with plant juices (anthotypes are “photographic images made with light-sensitive juices from plants”) and explains how the image forms: “Exposed areas of the coating fade, while covered areas retain their color.”

B.why_wrong: It explains how the image forms but never says what an anthotype is, which an unfamiliar audience would need.

C.why_wrong: It says who developed the process and when but not how an anthotype’s image forms.

D.why_wrong: It describes preparing the paper but stops before explaining how sunlight produces the image.

items.notes: Subject: arts and science (anthotypes, a nineteenth-century photographic process using plant juices). Real subject known without a search (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill); John Herschel’s 1842 work on plant-juice images is well documented.

review.note: John Herschel's 1842 plant-juice process is real; nothing invented is attributed to him

Kiruna is home to one of the world’s largest underground iron ore mines, and since the 2010s, many of its buildings have been moved to a new center about three kilometers east.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A moonbow, or lunar rainbow, forms when moonlight rather than sunlight is refracted by water droplets.
• Moonbows are frequently observed near waterfalls, such as Victoria Falls, on nights with a full moon.
• Moonlight is far fainter than sunlight.
• In dim conditions, the cells in the human eye that perceive color respond only weakly.
• To most observers, a moonbow looks like a pale white arc, but long-exposure photographs reveal its colors.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why moonbows usually look white to observers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Moonbows, which form when moonlight is refracted by water droplets, are frequently observed near waterfalls.
Although a moonbow looks like a pale white arc to most observers, long-exposure photographs reveal its colors.
